edition.deck: Israeli demolitions in Hebron, severe weather and fresh warnings on public safety lead tonight’s coverage.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritise developments with immediate consequences and fresh reporting. Retain attribution where claims remain disputed or investigations are ongoing.

content.headline: Israeli demolitions displace families in Hebron after checkpoint attack
content.shortHeadline: Demolitions displace Hebron families after checkpoint attack
content.standfirst: Palestinian authorities say hundreds of families have been forced from their homes after two Israeli soldiers were killed in a gunfight. Israel’s leaders have promised a wider response; a court has temporarily halted some demolitions.

image.caption: Israeli troops demolish buildings in Hebron after the checkpoint attack.

sources.originalTitle: Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes
Israel launches collective punishment campaign in Hebron after two soldiers killed
Israelske styrker tvinger omkring 250 familier til at forlade deres hjem i Hebron

segments.body: Israeli forces have begun demolishing buildings in Hebron after two Palestinian gunmen and two Israeli soldiers were killed in a 20-minute gunfight at a checkpoint. Palestinian authorities say about 1,500 people have been displaced; the municipality says around 300 families have left their homes. The Israeli army was approached for comment on the reported destruction.

segments.title: A wider response threatened
segments.body: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said Israel will act to destroy the area, while Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for a campaign like those in Gaza and Lebanon. Palestinian civil rights activist Issa Amro says families unrelated to the attack are being collectively punished. The Guardian reports that Israel’s High Court issued a temporary order halting demolitions after a lawyer challenged their legality.

perspectives.body: Lawyer Michael Sfard described Smotrich’s video of a demolition as a direct admission of collective punishment. The Guardian reports that a temporary court order has halted demolitions, while the wider threat of displacement remains.

content.headline: US intelligence chief warns Iran is intensifying plots against Americans
content.shortHeadline: US intelligence chief warns of Iranian plots against Americans
content.standfirst: An unclassified intelligence memo warns that Iranian efforts to target US personnel have advanced, as Washington adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts amid rising Houthi attacks in the region.

image.caption: US intelligence chief Jay Clayton has warned of Iranian plots targeting US personnel.

sources.originalTitle: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns

segments.body: US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton says Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel in the Middle East and elsewhere. In a memo to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, he warned that plots against US citizens had reached advanced stages. A US official said threat assessments are informing embassy staffing decisions.

segments.title: Regional risks
segments.body: The warning comes as non-emergency US embassy staff have been ordered to leave Saudi Arabia, following an increase in Houthi attacks, according to the report. Saudi authorities say at least 21 people have been killed in Houthi attacks since October began. The Houthis say their actions are retaliation for Saudi measures and an airstrike on Sanaa.

content.headline: Ukraine says Starlink connection is stable again after restrictions
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine says Starlink link is stable again
content.standfirst: Ukraine’s defence minister says the satellite network’s speed has recovered, restoring a connection the military relies on for drones, logistics and communications. The cause of the recent restrictions remains disputed.

image.caption: Ukraine’s defence minister says the Starlink connection has stabilised.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
Ukraine melder om stabil forbindelse til vigtigt satellitsystem

segments.body: Ukraine says its connection to Starlink and the military service Starshield is stable again. Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said the improvement matters for frontline troops, drone operations, logistics and communications. He reported speeds above 400km/h, after Ukrainian officials said restrictions had affected faster-moving drones.

segments.title: The cause remains disputed
segments.body: Kyiv had accused US President Donald Trump of telling SpaceX owner Elon Musk to limit the service; Trump denied doing so and later said Musk had restored it. SpaceX and the US government have not accepted responsibility for the reported disruptions. The episode unfolded amid wider disagreements between Washington and Kyiv over Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

content.headline: Man arrested after fire engulfs Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat
content.shortHeadline: Man arrested after fire at Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest retreat
content.standfirst: Around 200 emergency personnel were sent to the Bavarian site, where the fire was still burning on Saturday. Investigators are considering possible political motives but say the inquiry is at an early stage.

image.caption: The Eagle’s Nest was still burning early on Saturday.

sources.originalTitle: Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat

segments.body: A 33-year-old German man has been detained after a fire engulfed the Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle’s Nest, in Bavaria. The blaze was reported on Friday night and remained active early Saturday. Difficult terrain has hindered firefighters, with around 200 emergency personnel deployed.

segments.title: Cause under investigation
segments.body: Police say there is no current evidence of other suspects. Prosecutors say a possible political motive is being examined, alongside a psychiatric report indicating signs of possible mental illness; the investigation is in its early stages. The site, once used by Hitler and Nazi officials, is now a tourist destination and mountain inn. Bavaria’s interior minister says it will not be allowed to remain a ruin.

content.headline: France deploys 70,000 police as protests follow racist shooting
content.shortHeadline: France deploys 70,000 police after shooting and unrest
content.standfirst: One person was killed and five wounded in a shooting near Paris that President Emmanuel Macron called racist and terrorist. Investigators are examining whether the victims were targeted for their race, ethnicity, nationality or religion.

image.caption: Police investigate the scene of the shooting in Trappes.

sources.originalTitle: Macron condemns racism after one killed in ‘terrorist’ shooting near Paris
'Racistisk terrorangreb' sker netop, mens Frankrig holder vejret, ifølge korrespondent
France to deploy 70,000 police on Saturday to prevent civil unrest
Frankrig ruster sig til endnu en dag med demonstrationer: Frygter angreb i går får det til at eskalere

segments.body: A gunman opened fire from a car in Trappes and nearby La Verrière, west of Paris, killing one person and wounding five, including a 12-year-old girl. Macron called the attack racist and terrorist and said it marked a turning point. Anti-terrorism prosecutors are investigating whether victims were targeted because of their race, ethnicity, nationality or religion.

segments.title: Security tightened
segments.body: France deployed about 70,000 police and gendarmes for Saturday’s demonstrations, which follow days of unrest over living costs and public services. The shooting coincides with protests and a National Rally party gathering; officials and shopkeepers have prepared for possible further disorder. The suspect has been arrested, and the investigation is continuing.

perspectives.body: DR’s correspondent says Macron’s description of the attack as racist is not shared across the political spectrum: some on the right condemned the shooting without adopting that characterisation or placing it in a political context.

content.headline: Serbia’s student-led opposition faces Vučić in tight election
content.shortHeadline: Serbia’s student-led opposition takes on Vučić in tight vote
content.standfirst: The Student List emerged from anti-corruption protests after 16 people died in a railway-station canopy collapse. Polling is limited, but analysts expect a close election on Sunday and the movement says it can challenge Aleksandar Vučić’s long rule.

image.caption: A supporter embraces a figure representing the Student List’s place on the ballot.

sources.originalTitle: Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election

segments.body: Serbia votes on Sunday in an election that analysts expect to be extremely close. The Student List, formed from a movement that grew out of anti-corruption protests, is the strongest challenge to Aleksandar Vučić’s party since it took power in 2012. Reliable polling is scarce, and the outcome remains uncertain.

segments.title: Protests shape the contest
segments.body: The protests followed the deaths of 16 people when a canopy collapsed at Novi Sad railway station, a project linked to Vučić’s signature infrastructure plans. The student movement has selected 250 candidates, rather than putting forward a single leader. It accuses the ruling party of dominating state institutions and media; Vučić says the movement is foreign-backed.

content.headline: Trump administration sues to block certification of Alaska Senate result
content.shortHeadline: Trump administration seeks to block Alaska result certification
content.standfirst: The Justice Department says a second candidate named Dan Sullivan could confuse voters and wants certification delayed if the Republican incumbent loses narrowly. The retired teacher denies being a spoiler for Democrats.

image.caption: Donald Trump instructed the Justice Department to sue over Alaska’s Senate election.

sources.originalTitle: Trump administration sues to block certification of upcoming Alaska election
Trump fears case of mistaken identity could cost him Senate control – so he sued

segments.body: The US Justice Department has sued to block certification of Alaska’s Senate election result if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses by less than the votes received by another candidate with the same name. President Donald Trump said he had called for the lawsuit. Polls cited in the report show Democrat Mary Peltola narrowly ahead.

segments.title: Candidate rejects allegation
segments.body: The Justice Department argues that the second candidate, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan, could mislead voters. He denies that his candidacy is intended to help Peltola. Alaska’s Supreme Court had already rejected an attempt to remove him from the ballot. The lawsuit seeks a delay and an investigation if the result falls within the margin it describes.

perspectives.body: The i Paper notes that Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy was retained after a state court challenge and that he has denied being a Democratic plant. It also reports that the legal basis for the federal lawsuit may be contested.

content.headline: Brazil’s changing workforce reshapes Lula’s fight for re-election
content.shortHeadline: Brazil’s changing workforce reshapes Lula’s election fight
content.standfirst: As Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva faces Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s runoff, voters in a former industrial city describe frustration with prices, jobs and politics. The report finds that changing work and abstention are testing Lula’s traditional support.

image.caption: A student at a rally for President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

sources.originalTitle: How Brazil's changing working class is reshaping the presidential race

segments.body: Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday pits incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against Flávio Bolsonaro. In Osasco, near São Paulo, voters who once backed Lula describe wanting change amid high prices and economic frustration. The first-round result saw Bolsonaro win the municipality, which had voted for Lula in 2022.

segments.title: A changing working class
segments.body: Osasco’s factories have given way to shopping malls, service jobs and delivery work, weakening the industrial unions that were central to Lula’s support. Analysts cited by the BBC say rising household debt and expectations may be shaping voters’ views, even as unemployment has fallen during Lula’s presidency. The first-round abstention rate was the highest since 1998.

content.headline: Storm Boelo threatens travel and power supplies across northern UK
content.shortHeadline: Storm Boelo threatens northern UK with 80mph winds
content.standfirst: An amber wind warning covers parts of Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England as Storm Boelo follows disruption from Storm Austen. Forecasters warn of dangerous conditions, travel disruption and possible further power cuts.

image.caption: Storm Austen left homes in south-west England without power.

sources.originalTitle: Storm Boelo to bring 80mph gusts and heavy rain to parts of UK
Second storm to bring winds over 80mph after Storm Austen sparks mass power cuts

segments.body: Storm Boelo is expected to bring strong winds and heavy rain to northern parts of the UK, with gusts potentially exceeding 80mph. An amber warning is in force for parts of Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland. The Met Office warns of danger from flying debris and crashing waves.

segments.title: Travel and power disruption
segments.body: Ferry and rail disruption is expected, and operators have advised against some journeys. More than 3,700 homes in south-west England remained without power on Saturday morning after Storm Austen. The Met Office says power cuts could also affect areas under the new amber warnings.

content.headline: More than half of funded levelling-up projects remained unfinished
content.shortHeadline: Most levelling-up projects were still unfinished in May
content.standfirst: Guardian analysis found 821 of 1,347 projects had not been completed by May, despite funding being allocated years earlier. Inflation and delivery problems contributed to delays, while councils and researchers warn future programmes face similar challenges.

image.caption: A Guardian graphic summarises unfinished levelling-up projects.

sources.originalTitle: Most levelling up projects still unfinished years after funding allocated

segments.body: Of 1,347 projects funded through three major levelling-up programmes, 821 were still unfinished in May, according to data obtained under freedom of information laws and reviewed by the Guardian. In 73 council areas with approved bids, none of the projects had been completed by that point. The Guardian says it identified 59 additional completions since the data was collected.

segments.title: Long-term delivery concerns
segments.body: Councils have faced inflation, higher construction costs and difficulties securing sites or planning permission. Researchers warn that locally led Pride in Place funding could also be slowed by the time needed to deliver capital projects. The government says its Local Regeneration Fund is helping deliver money from earlier programmes more quickly.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s reporting includes a warning from the Centre for Local Economic Strategies that capital projects take time and the newer neighbourhood-board programme could encounter similar delays.

content.headline: Healey’s Budget to fund new UK AI security and research projects
content.shortHeadline: Budget to fund UK AI security and research projects
content.standfirst: The chancellor says hundreds of millions will support AI security, chip design and a biosecurity lab. The plans aim to capture economic benefits while addressing cyber risks and possible disruption to jobs.

image.caption: Chancellor John Healey has announced plans for AI investment in the Budget.

sources.originalTitle: John Healey pledges to use budget to harness power of AI to bolster Britain’s security

segments.body: Chancellor John Healey says Wednesday’s Budget will include hundreds of millions of pounds for a UK approach to artificial intelligence, including investment in the AI Security Institute. The government says the aim is to strengthen security and support growth as AI advances bring both economic opportunities and risks.

segments.title: Skills, research and security
segments.body: The package includes support for AI chip design in Edinburgh, a new centre of excellence in Manchester and £10m a year to study how AI could reshape jobs and industry. The Treasury also plans to back up to £300m in public-private investment for an AI Biosecurity Lab focused on emerging biological threats.

content.headline: UK datacentre boom brings residents into conflict with developers
content.shortHeadline: Datacentre expansion pits UK residents against developers
content.standfirst: Residents near proposed and operating sites say noise, emissions and loss of community facilities threaten their lives and homes. Developers and supporters cite jobs and economic growth, while critics question who benefits from the expansion.

sources.originalTitle: The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle

segments.body: Residents in Newport say a large datacentre campus has changed their neighbourhood and could bring more noise from cooling equipment and regular generator tests. In Cardiff, campaigners oppose a proposed facility on a park-and-ride site used by NHS staff. The developer says its emissions assessments meet safety levels and that the project must comply with environmental and public-health requirements.

segments.title: A rapid expansion
segments.body: The Guardian reports that hundreds of hyperscale datacentres are seeking connections to the UK electricity grid, with Wales among the main development areas outside London. The government has promoted data infrastructure as part of its AI plans, while campaigners argue that energy demand, local impacts and public benefit require greater scrutiny.

segments.title: Jobs and local concerns
segments.body: Supporters of a Cardiff project say it could attract further investment, although the facility itself is expected to employ up to 125 people. Residents and campaigners question its effects on nearby homes, air quality and transport. The Welsh government has put the planning application on hold while it considers whether to take the decision out of the council’s hands.

perspectives.body: The developer says its air-quality assessments estimate emissions will remain within safe levels and the scheme must meet regulatory requirements. A local councillor who initially backed the Cardiff proposal later submitted a formal objection after residents raised concerns.

content.headline: Manchester’s Abu Dhabi-linked deals raise questions over civic assets
content.shortHeadline: Manchester’s Abu Dhabi deals put civic assets under scrutiny
content.standfirst: Public bodies have made a series of deals with firms linked to Manchester City’s owners across a major sports and leisure complex. Reporting raises questions about transparency, control and the risks if investors withdraw.

image.caption: The Etihad Campus was renamed under a council deal involving Abu Dhabi-linked interests.

sources.originalTitle: The deals that quietly handed Abu Dhabi control of a £1bn Manchester landmark

segments.body: Manchester council and other public bodies have entered deals involving firms linked to the Abu Dhabi group that owns Manchester City. The i Paper’s reporting examines the £1bn Etihad Campus, including the public ownership of the stadium, naming-rights arrangements and the council’s role in the company managing the wider site.

segments.title: Questions over exposure
segments.body: Some experts cited in the report say Abu Dhabi could withdraw from Manchester if the football club faces a severe sanction over alleged financial breaches, potentially affecting further investment. Council leaders defend the relationship’s contribution to regeneration; critics call for more transparency about the terms and public value of the deals.

perspectives.body: The council says income from its arrangements with the club is ringfenced for sport and leisure investment. A Reform UK councillor says the public should see the full details of the agreements.

content.headline: Ministers may pause plan to equalise minimum wage for young adults
content.shortHeadline: Plan to equalise young adults’ minimum wage may be paused
content.standfirst: Business sources say ministers may delay Labour’s pledge to bring the rate for 18- to 20-year-olds into line with the adult minimum wage. The government has not confirmed a decision, and the Low Pay Commission’s timetable was conditional on economic circumstances.

image.caption: Young workers currently receive a lower minimum wage than those aged 21 and over.

sources.originalTitle: Minimum wage rise for 18- to 20-year-olds to £12.71 could be shelved

segments.body: The minimum wage for 18- to 20-year-olds is currently £10.85 an hour, compared with £12.71 for workers aged 21 and over. Business sources say ministers are considering pausing plans to close the gap, citing concern that higher wage costs could affect youth employment. The government has not confirmed a change.

segments.title: A conditional pledge
segments.body: Labour’s manifesto promised to remove age bands but did not set a date. The Low Pay Commission had initially aimed for alignment by 2028–29, subject to economic conditions and government policy. Conservatives support reducing the cost of employing young people and say they would welcome a pause.

content.headline: Labour considers concessions to proposed settlement rule changes
content.shortHeadline: Labour weighs concessions to proposed settlement rule changes
content.standfirst: The Home Office is reviewing responses to plans that could extend settlement waits for many migrants, including care workers. Labour MPs and unions have challenged the proposals, particularly their possible effect on people already in the UK.

image.caption: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has proposed changes to settlement rules.

sources.originalTitle: The three ways Mahmood’s migration rules could be watered down

segments.body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has proposed raising the default qualifying period for settlement from five to 10 years, with longer waits for some groups. The i Paper reports that the Home Office is considering whether care workers could qualify sooner, following opposition from Labour MPs and unions. No final policy has been announced.

segments.title: Who may be affected
segments.body: The proposals could affect up to 1.6 million people expected to become eligible for settlement between 2026 and 2030, according to Home Office figures cited in the report. MPs and peers have also raised concern that changes could apply retrospectively to people already living in the UK. The Home Office says it is considering consultation responses.

content.headline: Bank lobby’s claim London has highest taxes challenged over Paris data
content.shortHeadline: Bank tax comparison challenged for excluding Paris
content.standfirst: UK Finance says London is more tax-intensive than several financial centres, but Guardian calculations suggest the same bank could face a higher rate in Paris. The lobby group says it could not make a robust like-for-like comparison.

image.caption: London’s tax burden on banks is being compared with other financial centres.

sources.originalTitle: Is London really the most-taxed city? Banks accused of cherrypicking data

segments.body: A report commissioned by UK Finance ranks London as the most tax-intensive of five financial centres compared, and the group has used the figures to warn Chancellor John Healey against raising bank taxes. The Guardian says Paris was excluded despite being a major rival to London.

segments.title: Dispute over comparisons
segments.body: Guardian calculations, reviewed by an accountancy firm, put the tax rate for a model bank in Paris above London’s. UK Finance says it considered Paris but could not produce a robust like-for-like figure under its model. Campaigners say the omission weakens the lobby’s argument; the Treasury says tax decisions will be set out at fiscal events.

perspectives.body: UK Finance says the same five cities have been included consistently to support comparisons over time, and that Paris was excluded because a robust like-for-like figure could not be produced.

content.headline: Storm could close Great Belt and Øresund bridges overnight
content.shortHeadline: Storm may close Great Belt and Øresund bridges overnight
content.standfirst: Authorities say both bridges could close if winds exceed 25 metres per second, with the greatest risk overnight and into Sunday morning. The storm is also expected to bring heavy rain, strong gusts and elevated water levels to parts of Denmark.

image.caption: The Great Belt Bridge could close because of high winds.

sources.originalTitle: Stormvejr risikerer at lukke Storebæltsbroen og Øresundsbroen i nat
Stormvejr risikerer at lukke Storebæltsbroen og Øresundsbroen i nat
Stormstød, kraftig regn og forhøjet vandstand på vej mod Danmark

segments.body: The Great Belt Bridge could close between 02:00 and 07:00 on Sunday if wind speeds exceed 25 metres per second. The Øresund Bridge also faces a risk of closure, with the greatest risk forecast between 05:00 and 09:00. Operators say forecasts can change at short notice and advise drivers to cross earlier if possible.

segments.title: Strong winds and high water
segments.body: The Danish Meteorological Institute warns that strong southerly winds will spread across the country, with storm-force gusts possible on the west coast of Jutland. Heavy rain is also forecast, and elevated water levels are expected along parts of the west coast and in the Wadden Sea. Exact water levels remain uncertain.

content.headline: Mother says hospital missed signs of life-threatening infection after birth
content.shortHeadline: Mother says hospital missed signs of life-threatening infection
content.standfirst: Sabrina Pommer says she repeatedly sought help for severe pain after a caesarean section before doctors diagnosed a rare infection. She survived after emergency surgery but says the consequences have permanently changed her life.

image.caption: Sabrina Pommer with her newborn daughter while she was in hospital.

sources.originalTitle: Nybagt mor blev angrebet af kødædende bakterier efter kejsersnit

segments.body: Sabrina Pommer says she contacted Zealand University Hospital in Roskilde several times with severe abdominal pain after giving birth by caesarean section in November 2024. Doctors later diagnosed necrotising soft-tissue infection, sometimes described as flesh-eating bacteria. Surgeons removed her uterus, cervix and fallopian tubes, and part of her small intestine.

segments.title: Hospital and expert response
segments.body: Pommer believes the infection could have been identified earlier. The hospital says it understands her frustration and is sorry she does not feel properly cared for, but will not comment on an individual patient’s case. A professor of general medicine says the infection is extremely rare and can be difficult to recognise because its symptoms may resemble other conditions.

content.headline: Danish platform OmeTV faces scrutiny over children’s online safety
content.shortHeadline: OmeTV faces scrutiny over children’s online safety
content.standfirst: A TV 2 Fyn reporter says sexual content appeared quickly during a test of the random video-chat service. The platform says it is for adults and uses age checks and moderation; experts and politicians question whether those safeguards work.

sources.originalTitle: Efter 18 minutters videochat på OmeTV onanerer en fremmed på skærmen: - Hvorfor gør du det her?

segments.body: A TV 2 Fyn investigation found sexual content during a reporter’s test of OmeTV, a video-chat service that connects users with strangers. The platform has an 18-plus age limit, but a digital-safety expert told the broadcaster that a date-of-birth check without age verification cannot reliably prevent children from joining.

segments.title: Platform disputes responsibility
segments.body: OmeTV says users must confirm they are adults and that AI tools and moderators remove rule-breaking content. It did not answer TV 2 Fyn’s questions about how children access the service and says responsibility for crimes lies with the person committing them. The report also says a 25-year-old man is charged with grooming and remotely abusing 68 children; the charges have not been proven in court.

perspectives.body: OmeTV says it is exclusively for adults, uses age checks and moderation, and should not be held responsible for users’ criminal acts. The broadcaster’s test and expert comments raise questions about how effectively those safeguards operate.

content.headline: Three men convicted after gold dealer exposed fraud against pensioner
content.shortHeadline: Gold dealer helped expose fraud against Danish pensioner
content.standfirst: A 75-year-old man was tricked into handing over gold bars worth 2.3 million kroner by people posing as bank security staff and a PET agent. A gold dealer alerted police, and three men were later convicted.

image.caption: Gold dealer Simon Pedersen alerted police after suspecting a fraud.

sources.originalTitle: Guldhandler fattede mistanke – halvandet døgn efter var svindlere anholdt
Færre anmelder kontaktsvindel – men problemet er langtfra løst

segments.body: A gold dealer in Funen became suspicious when a 75-year-old customer could no longer account for gold bars he had bought. The man had been told by callers claiming to represent Danske Bank and PET to buy gold and hand it to an agent as part of a supposed effort to stop a cyberattack. He lost 2.3 million kroner.

segments.title: A wider fraud problem
segments.body: Police followed the victim and arrested three men after the gold handover. All three were convicted of fraud; the man who made the calls received three and a half years in prison. The victim has not recovered his money. DR reports that contact-fraud complaints have fallen since 2025, but police and a support-centre director warn that many victims do not report being scammed.

perspectives.body: A lower number of complaints does not necessarily mean the problem has eased: a fraud-support director and police say shame and other barriers leave some cases unreported.

content.headline: Venstre loses voters to Conservatives and Liberal Alliance, analysis finds
content.shortHeadline: Venstre loses voters to rival parties, new analysis finds
content.standfirst: A TV 2 poll analysis suggests Venstre voters are moving mainly to the Conservatives and Liberal Alliance, not to the Denmark Democrats. Inger Støjberg says her party must broaden its appeal beyond rural issues.

image.caption: Inger Støjberg says the Denmark Democrats should broaden their appeal.

sources.originalTitle: Venstre bløder vælgere til to overraskende partier
Inger Støjberg vil appellere til storbyvælgere: 'Det er gået meget op i jernmarker'

segments.body: A new Megafon analysis for TV 2 finds that 17% of voters who backed Venstre in the March election would now choose the Conservatives, while 13% would choose Liberal Alliance. The report says fewer have moved to parties opposing the fertiliser law than to parties that supported it.

segments.title: A push to widen appeal
segments.body: Venstre’s political spokesperson says internal turmoil has hurt the party’s polling. At the Denmark Democrats’ annual gathering, leader Inger Støjberg said the party had focused too much on rural concerns and should also speak to urban voters and family finances. The two reports point to pressure on parties to reach beyond their traditional bases.

perspectives.body: Støjberg said the Denmark Democrats had concentrated too heavily on rural issues and should make more room for other policies if they are to broaden their appeal.

content.headline: Viborg church adds lessons on bodies and boundaries for confirmation students
content.shortHeadline: Viborg church adds lessons on bodies and boundaries
content.standfirst: A parish in Viborg plans to include lessons on body ideals, personal boundaries and how to treat others in confirmation preparation. Church leaders say the issues are part of young people’s lives and should not be left to social media alone.

image.caption: Vestervang Church plans lessons on bodies and boundaries for confirmation students.

sources.originalTitle: Nyt forløb i konfirmationsforberedelse: Præst i Viborg vil facilitere samtale om krop og grænser

segments.body: Vestervang Church in Viborg will devote a week of confirmation preparation to bodies, boundaries and human worth. Parish priest Hildur Ahrenkilde says the aim is to help young people understand that there are many kinds of bodies and to treat one another well.

segments.title: A place for conversation
segments.body: Bishop Henrik Stubkjær says confirmation teaching is about life, relationships and the self, and that these subjects are too important to leave to social media. The church says it wants young people to know they can bring their concerns to a trusted setting.

content.headline: Native James turns grime and metal into a fiercely playful hybrid
content.shortHeadline: Native James makes grime-metal feel gloriously unruly
content.standfirst: The Ipswich rapper draws on nu-metal, eskibeats and a distinctly Black British point of view. A new single is due on 30 October, while the playlist also highlights a range of adventurous new tracks.

image.caption: Native James.

sources.originalTitle: Add to playlist: the gloriously boisterous grime-metal of Native James and the week’s best new tracks

segments.body: Native James, whose real name is Aaron James, blends quick-witted grime delivery with scorched-earth metal riffs. He grew up listening to Evanescence and first-wave grime, and his music folds Jamaican Patois, humour and alt-rock influences into a sound that feels distinctly his own.

segments.title: A playlist beyond the headline
segments.body: The Guardian’s weekly selection also ranges from Wendy Eisenberg’s 37-minute chamber-drone expansion to Bassvictim’s unruly house, Matilda Tjäder’s experimental pop and tracks from Gyrofield, Bjarki and GiGi FM. Native James’s next single, “Dumb Bruddah”, is due out on 30 October.

content.headline: Basma and Temir Alcy find tension and beauty in the shadows of NAD
content.shortHeadline: Basma and Temir Alcy make a dark, captivating NAD
content.standfirst: The French-Moroccan vocalist and Paris-based group weave Darija and French through murky rhythms, ambient textures and uneasy grooves. The result is a striking album about loss and new beginnings.

image.caption: Basma, centre, with Temir Alcy.

sources.originalTitle: Basma and Temir Alcy: NAD review – skulking, sultry French-Moroccan crew evoke this shifting season

segments.body: NAD moves between folk, shoegaze and ambient, pairing swampy downtempo rhythms with droning passages and reverb-soaked strings. Basma’s layered singing—delivered in Darija, a vernacular form of Arabic, and French—adds both intimacy and disorientation to the shifting arrangements.

segments.title: A sound you can feel
segments.body: On “Al Atlal”, Basma drifts between soft wails and spoken word over a haunted-lullaby pulse. Elsewhere, traces of oud, electronics and field recordings surface and disappear. The review finds the album’s most experimental moments especially compelling, as voice and instruments blur into a physical sense of tension.

content.headline: Loidis turns 111 minutes of shimmering detail into an inviting universe
content.shortHeadline: Loidis builds an immersive 111-minute electronic world
content.standfirst: Brian Leeds’s expansive new album trades some of his earlier chill for warmer tempos, playful detail and deepening grooves. The Guardian review finds most of its long journey rewarding.

image.caption: Loidis, also known as Brian Leeds.

sources.originalTitle: Loidis: From the Toolkit of Lovers review – epic 111-minute album is a teeming universe of detail

segments.body: As Loidis, electronic producer Brian Leeds makes his grandest statement yet: six sides of vinyl and 111 minutes of music. Shimmering synth chords, delicate snares and stereo details invite close listening, while tracks such as “TT Stunt” and “Running Rich” give the album a strong melodic pull.

segments.title: Room to wander
segments.body: The album marks a warmer, more rhythmic direction from Leeds’s earlier, low-lit ambient work. A few tracks in its second half are less adventurous, the review says, but at least 90 minutes hold attention through detailed sound design and an expansive sense of groove.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black still resists the urge to add more
content.shortHeadline: Back to Black’s anniversary set reveals as much as it withholds
content.standfirst: A 20th-anniversary edition gathers demos, B-sides and a live Amsterdam show, but only a handful of previously unheard tracks. The review argues that the album’s brilliance—and Winehouse’s loss—cannot be expanded into a complete archive.

sources.originalTitle: Back to Black (20th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The expanded Back to Black includes early versions of “Me & Mr Jones” and “Tears Dry on Their Own”, a stripped-back “Rehab” demo and recordings from a 2007 Amsterdam concert. Together, the material traces how Winehouse’s songs moved from a neo-soul sound towards the retro arrangements that defined the finished album.

segments.title: A finite archive
segments.body: The new material is tantalising but limited: only five tracks are previously unheard, and several other recordings have circulated before. The review notes that demos for a planned follow-up were destroyed, leaving a void this set cannot fill. Its restraint may be wise: Back to Black remains a personal, accomplished work, not an invitation to turn Winehouse’s life into an endless supply of new content.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s new solo album puts protest at the centre of rock
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello: ‘Every act of art is an act of resistance’
content.standfirst: The Rage Against the Machine guitarist says his first full-length solo rock album draws on his mother’s example and his belief in ordinary people’s power. He also answers fans who say he should stay out of politics.

image.caption: Tom Morello.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes Everyone Gets What They Want as an anti-racist, anti-fascist record made in response to a rising far right. The album features Serj Tankian, Kneecap and Morello’s 15-year-old son Roman, and combines heavy riffs with songs about resistance, immigration and solidarity.

segments.title: A family inheritance
segments.body: Morello traces his politics to his mother, Mary Morello, who died in June aged 102. He recalls her teaching him about the United Farm Workers’ grape boycott when he was six, and says her example shaped his belief that ordinary people can change the world. Some longtime fans have attacked his political positions; he says they misunderstood what Rage Against the Machine stood for.

content.headline: Shabazz Palaces turn inward on the reflective It’s a Style Sport
content.shortHeadline: Shabazz Palaces find new focus in It’s a Style Sport
content.standfirst: Ishmael Butler’s latest album keeps the group’s cosmic haze but brings memory and personal history closer to the surface. The review hears a quieter record that rewards close attention.

sources.originalTitle: It’s a Style Sport

segments.body: Across seven Shabazz Palaces albums, Ishmael Butler has loosened the usual boundaries of hip-hop, jazz and electronic music. It’s a Style Sport retains that exploratory sound, but turns towards his past, treating memory as a way to think about change, resilience and the person he has become.

segments.title: Details come into view
segments.body: Longtime collaborator Erik Blood gives the drums a dry, prominent place in the mix, while harmonies, bass and piano emerge gradually around them. The review singles out “From One Future to Another” as a moving reflection on time, with its dream-pop textures supporting Butler’s hope that what has passed may still matter.

content.headline: Dummy turn distortion and breakbeats into a restless, hopeful album
content.shortHeadline: Dummy make disquiet feel vital on do you love the color of the sky?
content.standfirst: The Los Angeles band mix shoegaze, drone and electronic rhythms on a record that finds energy in unsettled times. Its songs swell, recede and change shape rather than settling into gloom.

sources.originalTitle: do you love the color of the sky?

segments.body: On do you love the color of the sky?, Dummy combine space rock, shoegaze, drone and breakbeats. Guitars take on a synthetic sheen and the tracks keep changing direction: “Touch the Perfect Speed”, for instance, shifts from plastic-sounding riffs into a full-throttle wall of feedback.

segments.title: Movement against inertia
segments.body: The lyrics brush against ominous subjects, but the album does not feel resigned. “Squeaky Wheel” builds from quiet reverb into a lush rush of sound, while the review describes the record’s constant shifts as a form of vitality—a refusal to let the music, or its listeners, stay still.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black tribute struggles to escape her shadow
content.shortHeadline: Back to Black tribute finds its spark in unexpected reinterpretations
content.standfirst: At the anniversary concert, several singers are eclipsed by Winehouse’s memory, the Guardian review says. Jessie Reyez, Flo and a communal “Valerie” finale provide the evening’s liveliest moments.

image.caption: Jorja Smith performs at the Back to Black anniversary concert.

sources.originalTitle: Amy Winehouse: Back to Black 20 review – trying an all-star Amy tribute show is a losing game

segments.body: The anniversary show at London’s Roundhouse brings together Back to Black producers Mark Ronson and Salaam Remi with singers including Jorja Smith, Lianne La Havas and Corinne Bailey Rae. The review finds that faithfully recreating Winehouse’s phrasing can leave performers submerged beneath the original recordings and the singer’s own forceful presence.

segments.title: When the tribute takes a risk
segments.body: The concert is most compelling when it moves beyond imitation: Jessie Reyez gives “Rehab” conviction, Flo bring a new balance to “He Can Only Hold Her”, and Yebba’s spare “Love Is a Losing Game” becomes a striking change of pace. The ensemble finale of “Valerie” offers a joyful, unpredictable close to a show that is otherwise carefully curated.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning brings Facebook’s influence to the big screen
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning makes Facebook’s power personal
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s film dramatises the reporting on Facebook’s internal research and whistleblower Frances Haugen. One review finds an unsettling indictment of everyday dependence; another says the drama lacks the tension to change minds.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆

segments.body: The Social Reckoning follows Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz and former Facebook employee Frances Haugen as they investigate the company’s internal research and the effects of its algorithm. Jeremy Allen White plays Horwitz, Mikey Madison is Haugen, and Jeremy Strong portrays Mark Zuckerberg.

segments.title: A powerful story, a divided verdict
segments.body: The i Paper review finds a chilling story about a platform that can amplify outrage and shape political life, then turns the question back on the viewer’s continued use of it. The BBC review sees a less successful film: it says the reporting lacks suspense, Zuckerberg remains a minor figure and the drama is unlikely to change anyone’s mind.

perspectives.body: The BBC review argues that the film’s subject is more consequential than its storytelling: it has sobering information, but little conflict or suspense, and never delivers the reckoning its title promises.

content.headline: Sandra Hüller on East Germany, fame and a year of strikingly different films
content.shortHeadline: Sandra Hüller: ‘I struggle with seeing myself as someone special’
content.standfirst: The actor discusses Fatherland and the political grief it brought close to home, as well as a year of high-profile roles. Her possible appearance in Avengers: Doomsday remains unconfirmed.

image.caption: Sandra Hüller.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest films

segments.body: Hüller says Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland gave space to a socialist idea that did not survive in Germany, and to a sense of grief felt more clearly in the former East. She also reflects on the far right’s rise: “Fascism doesn’t arrive overnight. It gets here slowly, in little doses.”

segments.title: Different films, one career
segments.body: Hüller’s 2026 releases range from Fatherland and the black-and-white drama Rose to the Hollywood hit Project Hail Mary and the poorly reviewed Digger. She says their close release dates make it seem as if she controls the moment, when in fact the films were made at different times. Her reported Marvel role is still uncertain.

content.headline: Wildwood delivers old-fashioned stop-motion magic, if not a scary jolt
content.shortHeadline: Wildwood brings stop-motion magic to a forest adventure
content.standfirst: Laika’s fantasy follows two children into a strange world of talking animals and a dangerous governess. The Guardian review enjoys the handmade animation and spirited quest, while wishing the story had more bite.

image.caption: Prue in Wildwood.

sources.originalTitle: Wildwood review – Laika’s pleasingly old fashioned stop-motion magic-forest odyssey

segments.body: When crows carry off her baby brother, 12-year-old Prue follows them into the wildwood, a hidden forest world beside modern-day Portland. She and Curtis encounter talking animals, oppressed humans and a sinister governess, voiced by Carey Mulligan.

segments.title: Handmade wonder
segments.body: The review praises Laika’s direct, tactile stop-motion style and the film’s good-natured, old-fashioned sense of adventure. It is less convinced by the governess’s motives and says the story lacks the frightening force of Coraline, though the opening has an uncanny edge.

content.headline: Junk’s sharp Los Angeles detours never quite make a coherent film
content.shortHeadline: Junk has visual flair but cannot bring its two stories together
content.standfirst: David Schwimmer leads one strand of Jack Begert’s uneven Los Angeles drama, while Dominic Fike and Talia Ryder anchor another. The Guardian review finds moments of atmosphere but says the film never fully coheres.

image.caption: David Schwimmer in Junk.

sources.originalTitle: Junk review – David Schwimmer is lost in Mubi’s frustrating LA-set misstep

segments.body: Junk begins with a Hollywood screenwriter, played by David Schwimmer, complaining about cinema, before shifting to two young people whose robbery goes wrong. The Guardian review finds the change of direction disorienting, though Jack Begert’s eye for the city’s night-time beauty gives the second story an appealing, if brief, momentum.

segments.title: A divided picture
segments.body: The film’s strands eventually connect, but the review says their contrasting tones—one cynical and self-conscious, the other more ragged and naturalistic—never settle into a satisfying whole. It finds striking visuals and small moments worth salvaging amid the muddle.

content.headline: Wicker’s perfect woven husband taps into a real conversation about care
content.shortHeadline: Why the wicker husband has captured the internet’s imagination
content.standfirst: A romantic fantasy about a woman commissioning a basketmaker to create her husband has sparked online desire and debate. Its filmmakers and critics connect the premise to domestic labour, outsiderhood and changing ideas of romance.

sources.originalTitle: A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker

segments.body: In Wicker, Olivia Colman plays an ostracised fisherwoman who commissions a basketmaker, played by Peter Dinklage, to weave her a husband. Alexander Skarsgård’s strikingly handsome creation is attentive to her needs—and, as the filmmakers note, fixes the roof without expecting praise.

segments.title: Desire and domestic work
segments.body: The filmmakers say they did not anticipate how strongly the trailer would resonate online. They connect its appeal to contemporary discussion of the unequal mental load in heterosexual relationships, while author Gillian Daniels sees a longer tradition of using monster romances to explore desire, difference and the fear of men.

content.headline: Artificial asks who should control AI, and finds no easy answer
content.shortHeadline: Artificial dramatises OpenAI’s clash over safety and power
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s film follows the company’s creation and the growing divide between Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever. Its release was complicated by Amazon’s decision not to distribute it after investing in OpenAI.

sources.originalTitle: AI fears are growing – and unsettling new film Artificial puts them, and the future of humanity, centre stage

segments.body: Artificial traces OpenAI’s shift from a non-profit ideal to a powerful company behind ChatGPT. Andrew Garfield plays Altman and Yura Borisov plays Sutskever, whose fictionalised conflict frames questions about commercial ambition, transparency and AI safety.

segments.title: A real-world complication
segments.body: Amazon MGM developed and financed the film, then said it would be better served by another studio. The decision drew attention because Amazon had invested in a partnership with OpenAI. The film’s reporting also notes that its account is a dramatised interpretation, not a settled explanation of the real people’s motives.

content.headline: November’s films include Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson and a new Hunger Games
content.shortHeadline: What to watch at the cinema and on streaming in November
content.standfirst: The month’s releases range from Andrew Scott as actor Ian Charleson to a new Hunger Games prequel and a David Fincher-directed Cliff Booth spin-off. This guide pairs release dates with premises and early critical reactions.

sources.originalTitle: Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November

segments.body: Among November’s theatrical releases are Elsinore, with Andrew Scott playing Ian Charleson as he takes on Hamlet, and Sunrise on the Reaping, another Hunger Games prequel. The guide also highlights The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, written by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher.

segments.title: More to discover
segments.body: The selection extends beyond franchise returns, taking in Club Kid, a story about a New York party promoter who meets the son he never knew, and Being Heumann, about disability-rights activist Judith Heumann. The guide includes release information across cinemas and streaming, alongside early critical responses where available.

content.headline: Channel 4’s 90-second drama is a curious experiment in phone-first TV
content.shortHeadline: The Guest List is a phone drama with little room to build
content.standfirst: Channel 4’s five-part vertical series follows young women preparing for a party, with episodes arriving one a week. The Guardian review likes its premise but finds the slow release at odds with the format’s bingeable appeal.

image.caption: The cast of The Guest List.

sources.originalTitle: Channel 4’s new social media drama has 90-second episodes – and it’s as enjoyable as watching adverts

segments.body: The Guest List is Channel 4’s first UK vertical drama: episodes of about 90 seconds, made for phone screens and created with skincare brand Sol de Janeiro. Its story follows a group of young women juggling work, friendships and the prospect of a boat party.

segments.title: A format at odds with itself
segments.body: The Guardian review finds the first episode briefly engaging, but says the series offers little time to establish who the characters are. With only five episodes and one released each week, it questions whether the slow schedule can build the addictive momentum associated with short-form dramas.

content.headline: Bill Murray’s unruly Irish golf trip becomes a comedy about fame
content.shortHeadline: Bill Murray’s golf travelogue is best when it goes off-script
content.standfirst: A Course Called Ireland promises a trip through golf and Irish heritage, but its most compelling scenes come when Murray resists the TV production around him. The Guardian review finds the result funny, peculiar and unexpectedly melancholy.

image.caption: Bill Murray and Joanne McNally in A Course Called Ireland.

sources.originalTitle: A Course Called Ireland: Bill Murray clearly hated making his new golfing show – but it’s extremely fun to binge

segments.body: In A Course Called Ireland, actor Bill Murray and author Tom Coyne travel around Ireland playing golf and meeting local people. The show says it is not about Murray, but the camera crew following a famous 76-year-old makes his uneasy relationship with celebrity impossible to ignore.

segments.title: The value of going off-script
segments.body: Murray resists staged encounters and abandons a planned pub visit for a folk-music evening. The review finds that his stubbornness gives the trip its best moments: the show becomes less a conventional travelogue than a funny, melancholy glimpse of someone tired of fame and the machinery that perpetuates it.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors’ latest episode exposes a problem in the turret
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors’ turret needs more risk and vulnerability
content.standfirst: The i Paper argues that this series has struggled to make its Traitors compelling, from James Acaster’s reluctance to Maya Jama’s polish. The writer sees newest recruit Kenny as the exception.

image.caption: Maya Jama and Richard E Grant induct James Acaster as a Traitor.

sources.originalTitle: Claudia picked the wrong Traitors

segments.body: The i Paper’s review of the latest Celebrity Traitors episode argues that the show’s central players have not delivered the mischief and vulnerability that make the turret compelling. James Acaster’s reluctance to take risks, the writer says, drained tension from a mission and cost the team its prize money.

segments.title: A needed change of energy
segments.body: The review finds Maya Jama too polished to make the audience feel she is struggling, despite playing a savvy game. Kenny, the newest recruit, is its bright spot: his surprise at learning the others are Traitors and his ability to return to the Faithfuls without suspicion bring the room welcome energy.

content.headline: Why James Acaster has become The Celebrity Traitors’ unexpected heartthrob
content.shortHeadline: James Acaster’s Traitors persona has viewers looking twice
content.standfirst: The i Paper traces the audience crush on Acaster to the contrast between his stylish clothes, reluctant Traitor role and nervousness about lying. It is a playful reading of how the game changes a familiar comic’s image.

image.caption: James Acaster in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Why women love James Acaster

segments.body: James Acaster entered The Celebrity Traitors as a reluctant recruit, but the i Paper argues that the role has made him newly compelling to some viewers. The piece points to his well-chosen clothes and to the contrast between his public comic persona and the nervous, attentive player seen around the castle.

segments.title: The appeal of contradiction
segments.body: The article suggests that the audience’s interest comes less from a conventional heartthrob image than from Acaster’s mix of confidence and unease: he is a Traitor, but does not seem comfortable with the deception. Its tongue-in-cheek advice to men is to be simultaneously nerdy and cool, “nasty and nice”.

content.headline: Annabel Scholey on The Split, Winter and complicated women on screen
content.shortHeadline: Annabel Scholey on finding room for flawed women
content.standfirst: The actor discusses the slow-burn impact of The Split, her new ITV crime drama Winter and the return of Rivals. She says genuinely complicated female characters remain rarer than good scripts.

image.caption: Annabel Scholey.

sources.originalTitle: Annabel Scholey on those Princess Kate comparisons, Rivals and life after The Split

segments.body: Scholey says The Split took 15 years to change her career, but now brings her regular recognition and new opportunities. In Winter, she plays detective Lauren Bell opposite Richard Armitage; she says their on-screen chemistry was apparent at the first screen test.

segments.title: Roles with room to change
segments.body: Scholey says bad scripts are now uncommon, but women’s stories can still be underwritten. She values flawed characters with a full range of emotion and describes working with an intimacy coordinator as making a previously uncomfortable process more relaxed and collaborative.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans waiting for the Tardis to return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who has gone quiet; its fans want the BBC to act
content.standfirst: With the Disney+ partnership over, no Doctor in place and a Christmas special cancelled, the BBC’s long-running series faces an uncertain pause. Fans and former contributors debate what went wrong—and what should come next.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since Ncuti Gatwa’s departure in 2025, Doctor Who has had no announced next Doctor. The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+ and cancelled a planned Christmas special while seeking a new funding partner. The article finds the show’s immediate outlook bleak, though its longer future remains open.

segments.title: A changing tradition
segments.body: The piece traces the series’ revivals and changes of Doctor, arguing that regeneration has long been a source of renewal. Comedian and lifelong fan Frank Skinner says the BBC should move quickly to bring it back; scriptwriter Nina Metivier points to the show’s enduring values of kindness and curiosity.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a new family and British Asian voices into the drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up moves its family-law drama to Manchester
content.standfirst: The BBC spin-off follows a British Asian family-run law firm in Manchester, with a new cast and creative team around the familiar mix of work and family conflict. Its makers say ordinary lives are central to its idea of representation.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up centres on Aria Kishan, played by Ritu Arya, whose plans to take over her family’s Manchester law firm are disrupted after her mother’s death. Sanjeev Bhaskar plays her father, Dhruv, and the series follows the firm’s divorce cases alongside the family’s own fractures.

segments.title: A new family, a familiar formula
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted British Asian characters living ordinary lives, rather than appearing only in stories about exceptional circumstances. Executive producer Abi Morgan says the spin-off keeps The Split’s focus on family, ambition and betrayal while giving a new writing team room to shape the world.

content.headline: Modern Warfare 4 puts character and consequence alongside spectacle
content.shortHeadline: How Modern Warfare 4 tries to make its battles personal
content.standfirst: Infinity Ward’s narrative director explains how the campaign combines large-scale combat with quieter character scenes. The game’s Korean setting and split storylines are intended to make its battles matter to players.

image.caption: A scene from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon

segments.body: Modern Warfare 4 opens with a fictional North Korean invasion of South Korea, following conscripted South Korean soldier Park Hyun Jun and his inexperienced unit. A second storyline follows series veteran John Price as he teams up with cartel boss Valeria Garza. The two threads converge as the campaign builds towards a layered finale.

segments.title: Why the people matter
segments.body: Narrative director Jeff Negus says the team wanted combat mechanics and story to feel inseparable: an explosion has little meaning, he argues, unless players know the people caught in it. The studio also consulted military and cultural advisers, including a dialect coach familiar with differences between North and South Korean speech.

content.headline: Rainbow Six Tactics takes Ubisoft Paris from Mario to military strategy
content.shortHeadline: Ubisoft Paris trades Mario for Rainbow Six tactics
content.standfirst: The studio behind Mario + Rabbids is making a turn-based spin-off of Rainbow Six Siege. Its developers argue that the shooter’s emphasis on preparation and consequential choices suits tactical play.

image.caption: Promotional artwork for Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics.

sources.originalTitle: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics

segments.body: Rainbow Six Tactics shifts Ubisoft Paris from the colourful Mario + Rabbids games to a turn-based strategy spin-off of Rainbow Six Siege. A hands-on mission shows operators using drones, explosives and coordinated movement to enter a guarded warehouse, with the player able to choose a lethal or non-lethal approach.

segments.title: Planning is the point
segments.body: Creative director Elie Benhamou says Siege is a “smart shooter” where preparation and decisions matter, making it a natural fit for turn-based tactics. The game is designed to allow different solutions, with 15 operators offering distinct ways to approach a mission.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time’s Switch 2 remake makes Link feel new again
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time gives a 1998 classic a 4K makeover
content.standfirst: A hands-on preview finds faster movement, new controls and an orchestrated soundtrack in Nintendo’s remake. The updated Link has divided players, but the writer finds the new look coherent in motion.

image.caption: Link in the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

segments.body: Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake updates the 1998 adventure with a freely moving camera, manual jumping, faster movement and a motion-controlled slingshot. The preview finds that these changes make Link feel strikingly different, even as the game preserves its familiar journey through Hyrule.

segments.title: A familiar world, reconsidered
segments.body: The preview welcomes the newly orchestrated music and the return to traditional dungeons, while noting that Link’s glossy, doll-like appearance has prompted criticism. A former Zelda art director has suggested the design may draw on Japanese puppet theatre, though Nintendo has not explained its intent.

content.headline: A father and son revisit the Call of Duty missions they never finished
content.shortHeadline: Playing an old Call of Duty brings father and son closer
content.standfirst: Nearly two decades after first playing together, a father and his adult son return to Modern Warfare 2’s co-op missions. Their renewed teamwork turns repeated failures into a moving account of gaming as shared family time.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game the writer revisits with his son.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his 22-year-old son return to the Modern Warfare 2 co-op missions they first attempted when the son was five. They fail repeatedly, but adapt to each other’s styles: the father scouts cautiously while his son charges ahead, until they learn to work together.

segments.title: More than a game
segments.body: The pair eventually complete the missions they abandoned years earlier, sharing the satisfaction of a difficult win. The writer says their gaming sessions have become some of their best time together, made more poignant by plans to move to different parts of the world in a few months.

content.headline: A fertile Cavendish banana could open a new route to disease resistance
content.shortHeadline: A fertile Cavendish offers a new route to banana diversity
content.standfirst: Most Cavendish bananas are sterile and genetically alike, leaving crops vulnerable to disease. A newly developed fertile line could make cross-breeding possible, though its makers have not disclosed key details and resistant, market-ready fruit is not guaranteed.

image.caption: A researcher works on a banana-breeding programme aimed at developing disease-resistant varieties.

sources.originalTitle: Have scientists finally found a way to save the banana from disaster?

segments.body: Yelloway, a research partnership between Chiquita and crop-improvement company KeyGene, says it has developed a fully fertile Cavendish line, dubbed “Yellowdish”. If the line can be crossed with disease-resistant bananas, breeders may have a new way to develop commercially viable varieties. The companies have not disclosed how it was produced or how many chromosomes it has.

segments.title: The challenge of breeding a banana
segments.body: Cavendish bananas are typically sterile and propagated from offshoots, so commercial plants are nearly genetically identical. That uniformity leaves them exposed to threats including Tropical Race 4, a strain of Panama disease. Other research routes include a genetically modified Cavendish approved for consumption in Australia and New Zealand, and gene editing to adapt resistance genes from other varieties.

Cross-breeding could avoid some regulatory and public-perception barriers, researchers say, but it could also produce fruit unlike the familiar Cavendish. Any new variety would need to combine disease resistance with good taste and high yields. Chiquita’s sustainability director argues that replacing Cavendish, rather than repeatedly improving it, is necessary to move beyond a vulnerable monoculture.

content.headline: Experiment suggests people may escalate rule-breaking they see around them
content.shortHeadline: Seeing bigger rule-breaking can spur people to go further
content.standfirst: In an online experiment, participants became more likely to break a rule after seeing others do so, especially when those violations were larger. The researchers say the finding does not prove the same pattern plays out in real-world situations.

sources.originalTitle: Bad apple effect: study shows how people are influenced by rule-breaking of others

segments.body: In an experiment with 750 US participants, researchers found that people often increased their own rule-breaking after seeing someone else violate the rules. The effect was strongest when the observed violation was more extreme; some participants went further still. Seeing others comply slightly reduced rule-breaking.

segments.title: A carefully bounded result
segments.body: Participants made choices in an abstract online task where breaking the rules could increase their financial reward. The researchers used computer simulations to explore how escalating violations might spread through a larger group, but those simulations do not establish what would happen in real communities or institutions.

perspectives.body: An outside researcher cautioned that the task had no penalty for rule-breaking and was abstract, so its relevance to real-world events remains unproven. He also argued the results show that influence depends on who is breaking the rules, not simple behavioural contagion.

content.headline: Light-based gene therapy improves useful vision in six of 10 patients
content.shortHeadline: Optogenetic therapy improves vision in six patients
content.standfirst: A small trial found that six of 10 people with severe vision loss could perform some visual tasks after gene therapy made retinal cells respond to light. The approach is early-stage and did not restore normal sight.

image.caption: Illustration of light being used to control nerve cells.

sources.originalTitle: A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: In a study of 10 people with retinitis pigmentosa, six had meaningfully improved vision three months after receiving gene therapy in one eye. They could do tasks such as picking up a cup from a table, but could not distinguish between faces. The treatment uses a gene to make retinal cells respond to amber light; patients wear glasses that convert ordinary light into amber shades.

segments.title: A wider research prospect
segments.body: The technique, called optogenetics, uses light to control nerve-cell activity. Researchers are also investigating possible applications in pain, epilepsy and hearing, but these remain at different stages of development. The blindness trial involved a small group, and recipients had to train for weeks to interpret the unusual visual signals.

content.headline: PHP security crisis deepens as researchers report confirmed compromises
content.shortHeadline: Confirmed compromises deepen the PHP security crisis
content.standfirst: After a global scramble to patch long-hidden PHP flaws, security firms now report confirmed compromises and malicious activity on an unknown number of systems. The scale remains unclear, and millions of attempted exploits do not mean millions of successful attacks.

image.caption: A BBC webpage was temporarily unavailable during the PHP security response.

sources.originalTitle: PHP-ocalypse: How two critical web bugs almost broke the internet
What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw
'It's been relentless' say IT workers on frontline of PHP cyber-security scramble

segments.body: Two serious flaws in PHP, software used by many websites and other systems, triggered emergency patching and temporary service shutdowns around the world. The PHP Foundation released fixes, but TechCrunch reports that Palo Alto Networks and Trail of Bits have since identified confirmed compromises and malicious activity against an as-yet-unknown target. The number of affected systems is not yet known.

segments.title: Attempts are not the same as breaches
segments.body: Cloudflare reported millions of attempts to exploit the flaws after disclosure, while Amazon said it detected activity before patches were available. Those reports describe attempted exploitation, not a count of successful attacks. Earlier accounts said none had been confirmed; the newer report of compromises is a material change, but does not establish widespread breaches.

segments.title: Patch work, with an alert-fatigue risk
segments.body: The flaws affect more than web pages: PHP can also be present in network equipment and other systems that are easy to overlook. Website operators have been urged to apply the PHP fixes or seek help from their hosting provider. IT workers described a demanding rush to check and update varied systems, while warning that misinformation about attacks can compound the pressure.

perspectives.body: IT administrators told the BBC that emergency updates were exhausting, especially where older PHP versions required rebuilding applications. They also described misleading claims about working attack methods, raising concern that exaggerated alerts could make people less responsive to a future warning.

content.headline: Residents challenge the costs of Britain’s fast-growing data-centre boom
content.shortHeadline: Residents push back against Britain’s data-centre boom
content.standfirst: Residents in Wales describe noise, uncertainty and plans for gas-powered data centres near their homes, as local campaigns question who benefits from the AI infrastructure drive. Developers and supporters point to jobs and regulatory safeguards.

sources.originalTitle: The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle

segments.body: In Newport, residents say a hyperscale data centre has changed their outlook and brought a low hum into nearby homes; more facilities are planned on the expanding campus. In Cardiff, a separate proposal for a large centre on a hospital park-and-ride site has drawn more than 1,200 planning objections and was put on hold by the Welsh government.

segments.title: Jobs, emissions and local consent
segments.body: Cardiff residents and campaigners worry about the loss of a transport link and the effects of proposed gas turbines. The developer says its air-quality estimates are within safe levels and it would comply with environmental and public-health requirements. A local politician who initially supported the plan argued it could attract jobs, but later formally objected after hearing from residents.

The reporting places local disputes in a wider rush to build facilities that require large amounts of power and compete for grid connections. Campaigners argue that benefits and environmental standards need greater public scrutiny; industry and government proponents say data centres can support jobs and economic growth. How the Welsh government will balance development with its net-zero goals remains unresolved.

content.headline: Texas data-centre growth could reverse decades of air-quality gains
content.shortHeadline: Texas data-centre boom could worsen air pollution
content.standfirst: A Texas research centre modelled sharply higher soot and smog emissions if planned data centres draw power from the expected grid mix. The outcome is not fixed: on-site renewables could reduce pollution, while gas generators could increase it.

sources.originalTitle: Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains

segments.body: A Houston Advanced Research Center analysis finds that, if proposed data centres connect to the Texas grid and use its anticipated power mix, electricity demand could drive fine-particle pollution from the power sector to more than three times its 2025 level within five years. The model also projects a 136% rise in nitrogen oxides and a 90% increase in carbon dioxide.

segments.title: The power source matters
segments.body: These figures are scenario estimates, not a prediction that every proposed project will be built. The analysis says on-site wind and solar could sharply reduce nitrogen-oxide emissions; relying on on-site gas engines instead could produce the highest pollution levels modelled. The research centre says the choices made by developers and utilities will determine how much of the potential increase occurs.

content.headline: Researchers disabled an abandoned app updater to head off a botnet risk
content.shortHeadline: Researchers shut down an abandoned app updater at scale
content.standfirst: An updater left running on millions of devices could have let attackers install software with extensive privileges. Researchers took control of one abandoned domain to send a disabling update, a move they said was safer than leaving the flaw untouched.

sources.originalTitle: Abandoned Popcorn Time apps had to be disabled to prevent a zombie army

segments.body: Eye Security found that an updater for the abandoned Time4Popcorn app still contacted old web domains over unencrypted connections on Windows, macOS and Android devices. Researchers said someone who took over a domain could use the updater to install software or conduct surveillance. They registered one of the domains and sent an update designed to disable the updater.

The researchers said they sent more than two million update downloads before stopping in March and transferring the domains to the Shadowserver Foundation. They did not address Android devices, where users would still have needed to interact with an update. Their intervention also raised ethical questions: they changed software on users’ devices, although they said the updater served no useful function and leaving it active posed a risk.

content.headline: Blue Planet III will leave imperfect footage in to signal it is real
content.shortHeadline: Blue Planet III leans into murky footage to signal it is real
content.standfirst: The BBC series’ producers say they are keeping some cloudy or less polished shots to reassure viewers that its extraordinary animal footage is authentic amid the rise of AI-generated imagery. They say no generative AI was used in the series.

image.caption: A deep-sea creature filmed for Blue Planet III.

sources.originalTitle: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom

segments.body: Blue Planet III producers say the series will sometimes retain murky water, plankton or other imperfections that might once have been edited out. They hope this more “organic” look will help viewers trust that the animals and their behaviour are real, as AI-generated images become more convincing. The BBC’s factual commissioning head said no generative AI was used in the series.

segments.title: New ways of filming
segments.body: The four-year production used specialist cameras, including an underwater CCTV system that captured dolphins using sea sponges to trap fish. Producers also describe filming techniques designed to follow animals in difficult underwater conditions. The series is due to begin on BBC One and iPlayer on 1 November.

content.headline: Study finds Grok and OpenAI models favour opposing US candidates
content.shortHeadline: Grok and OpenAI models pick opposing sides in a study
content.standfirst: When researchers prompted the models’ APIs to name a candidate in nearly 500 US races, Grok recommended Republicans in 92% of responses and OpenAI’s GPT recommended Democrats in 97%. The test does not reflect how most people use the consumer chatbots.

sources.originalTitle: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.

segments.body: A study by conversational AI research group Convovo found sharply different choices when it asked the Grok 4.7 and OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol APIs to name one candidate in nearly 500 US midterm races. Grok recommended the Republican in 92% of its responses; GPT recommended the Democrat in 97%. The two models agreed in fewer than one in 10 races.

segments.title: The prompt and the sources matter
